opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. The starting point is a puzzle: data like images or text live in enormous dimensions, so learning a generic function should require an astronomical number of examples. That is the curse of dimensionality. Yet deep networks learn from a manageable amount of data. So the data must have structure that makes learning possible, and we want to know what that structure is and how networks exploit it.

One natural hypothesis is that data are hierarchical and compositional. A sentence is made of phrases, phrases of words, words of letters. An image is made of objects, objects of parts, parts of edges. Context-free grammars are a clean way to capture that. So we built a simplified, controllable version that we call the Random Hierarchy Model. You have a class label at the top, and a set of production rules generates the data downward, layer by layer, until you reach the visible tokens. The key ingredient is that several different low-level combinations can stand for the same higher-level symbol. These are synonyms, in a sense. Because the rules are random, there is no shortcut. The only way to solve the task is to actually discover the hidden hierarchy.

What makes this useful is that we control everything: the depth, the branching, the vocabulary size, the number of synonyms. So we can ask precise questions. How many examples does a network need? What has it learned internally when it succeeds?

The answer turned out to be quite illuminating. A shallow network, or a method that ignores the hierarchy, needs a number of samples that grows exponentially with the size of the input. A deep network needs only a number that grows polynomially. The mechanism is this. Low-level tuples that are synonyms have the same correlations with the label, or with other parts of the input. Once you have enough data to detect those correlations above the sampling noise, you can group synonyms together. The network then builds a representation that is invariant to which synonym was used. In other words, it has formed an abstraction, a latent variable one level up. Then it repeats the same process at the next level, and so on up the tree. We can predict the sample complexity from this argument, and it matches what we see when we train networks.

We can also check directly that the abstraction is there. We probe the hidden layers and measure how much the representation changes when you swap one synonym for another. Right at the point where the test error drops, those representations become insensitive to synonym exchanges. So learning the task and acquiring the abstraction happen together. They are essentially the same event.

This has implications beyond classification. In next-token prediction, the same correlation argument tells you that as the training set grows, the model can resolve correlations at longer and longer distances. That means it builds deeper levels of the hierarchy step by step. This gives a picture of why test loss improves as a power law with data, and why capabilities might seem to emerge in stages. We have also used these models to study diffusion. There, if you add noise and then denoise, you see a kind of phase transition. Low-level features change first, and at some noise level the high-level class itself can flip, which shows the model is manipulating the hierarchy itself.

So the grammar is a tool, a kind of toy universe. It is rich enough to have the property we think matters in real data, which is hierarchical compositionality with invariances, and simple enough that we can actually compute things. It lets us move from saying "deep networks learn abstractions" as a slogan to having a quantitative theory of when and how they do it.

fable-5.1.text:
So the starting point is that we don't really have a good theory of why deep networks learn anything from data that is, in principle, extremely high dimensional. If you think of an image, or a sentence, the number of possible inputs is astronomical, and the curse of dimensionality tells you that you should need an exponential number of examples to learn anything. And yet these models learn with a number of samples that is large, but nowhere near exponential. So there has to be structure in the data that the network exploits, and the natural hypothesis is that this structure is hierarchical and compositional. A sentence is made of phrases, phrases are made of words, words are made of letters. An image is made of objects, objects of parts, parts of edges. And the hope is that the network builds a hierarchy of representations that mirrors the hierarchy of the data.

The problem with testing that on real data is that you don't know the true structure. You can't say "this is the right abstraction at level three" because nobody wrote it down. So what we do is we generate the data ourselves with a model where we know everything. We take a simple context-free grammar, something like a tree. You start from a root symbol, and you have production rules that say this symbol becomes a pair, or a triple, of symbols at the next level, and so on down for a few levels until you reach the leaves, which are the actual tokens you see. We make it random, so the rules are drawn at random, and crucially we make it ambiguous, meaning the same low-level pattern can be generated by several different high-level symbols. That ambiguity is what makes the task non-trivial, because you cannot just read the high-level label off a local piece of the input, you need to use the context.

Then we train a network, either a convolutional network for a classification version where the label is the root, or a transformer in a masked or next-token prediction setting, and we ask very concrete questions. How many training points do you need before the network's performance jumps? What does it look like inside the network when that happens? And because we control the grammar, we can actually compute the answer. We can say the right latent variable at level two is this one, and then check whether the hidden representations become invariant to exchanging two low-level patterns that correspond to the same high-level symbol. That invariance is, to me, what an abstraction means in this setting. You've stopped caring about which synonym was used and you only care about the meaning.

And what we find is quite striking. The sample complexity is polynomial in the input size, not exponential, which is the first thing you want. And it scales roughly like the number of synonyms raised to the number of levels in the tree, which you can derive from a very simple argument. The argument is that to learn a given level of the hierarchy, you need to detect correlations between a low-level pattern and the label, or the next token, and those correlations are weak because of the ambiguity, so you need enough data to see them above the noise. Once you have enough data to resolve one level, you can collapse it, the problem becomes effectively smaller, and you go to the next level. So learning is a kind of clustering, bottom-up, where the network builds one layer of abstraction after another, and each one is triggered by having enough samples to see the correlations at that scale.

What's nice is that this is not just a story, we see it in the dynamics. If you train a transformer with next-token prediction and look at how the representations evolve, the low-level abstractions appear first, and higher ones appear later, in stages. And if you look at the correlations in the data at the corresponding scales, they match the point where the network gets each level. The same picture also tells you something about generation. If you sample from a model that has only learned up to some level, it produces text that is locally coherent but globally meaningless, which is exactly what people observe with undertrained language models. So the toy model captures that phenomenology, and it gives you a precise, quantitative handle on it. Of course, it's a simplification, real language is not a random context-free grammar. But I think if you want to understand abstraction, you first need a case where you can say what abstraction is, and this is one of the few where you can.

astra-6.text:
The advantage of a synthetic grammar is that we know the underlying structure that generates the data. With natural language, it is much harder to say precisely what abstraction a network should discover.

Imagine a hierarchy of rules. An abstract symbol can be replaced by several different combinations of symbols at the next level, and those symbols are expanded again until you obtain a sequence of observable tokens. The network sees only those tokens. It does not see the hidden symbols or the rules.

Now, several different sequences can correspond to the same hidden symbol. So we can ask whether the network learns that these sequences play the same role. Does its representation capture the underlying category, despite differences in the particular tokens? And can it use that category in combinations it has not encountered during training?

You can test this by changing the surface realization while preserving the hidden structure, and examining both the network’s predictions and its internal representations. You can also vary the amount of training data and the depth of the grammar to study when these properties emerge.

The important distinction is between remembering examples and discovering equivalences that the generative rules imply. These controlled settings let us make that distinction much more precise. They don’t reproduce all of language, of course, but they give us a way to study the acquisition of hierarchical abstractions as a concrete learning problem.

sol-6.1.text:
The advantage of a synthetic grammar is that we know exactly what the underlying abstractions are. We construct data from a hierarchy of rules: a high-level symbol can be replaced by several lower-level symbols, and those can be expanded again, until we obtain a sequence of observable tokens. The network only sees those tokens. It does not see the hidden symbols or the rules that generated them.

Then we can ask whether learning to predict the data leads the network to recover that hidden structure. For example, different groups of tokens may be generated by the same hidden symbol. They look different at the surface, but they play the same role in the grammar. Does the network learn to treat them as equivalent? Can it generalize to combinations that it has never encountered during training?

That gives us a controlled way to distinguish learning an abstraction from memorizing examples. We can vary the depth of the hierarchy, the number of alternative rules, and the amount of training data, and examine when generalization appears. We can also inspect the representations to see whether they encode the hidden grammatical categories.

The point is not that these grammars capture all of language. It is that they let us study a precise question: under what conditions does prediction force a network to discover the latent organization of its data?
